title: Lalla's two names
hookLine: Hindus call her Lalleshwari, Muslims Lal Arifa, and a Sufi saint asked God for what she had
tomorrow: a princess turns down her palace's god. who does she choose?

lines: RAY ANSWERED TO ALL OF THEM.
cards: Sunday lunch at Theo's parents' house. His grandpa called him Teddy all through the meal, his sister called him Theodore, and Zoe, who calls him Theo, almost corrected them both.
Afterward, on his own porch, Ray laughed: his students called him three different things, and he answered to all of them. Lalla has more than one name too. Hindus call her Lalleshwari.
Muslims call her Lal Arifa. Why both?

teach.b: Because both communities claim her, and each honored her in its own words of honor. To Kashmiri Hindus she's Lalleshwari, Lalla the Lady, ishwari, a word used for a goddess.

teach.h: LAL ARIFA: THE ONE WHO KNOWS GOD.
teach.b: To Kashmiri Muslims she's Lal Arifa: in Sufi language an arif is one who knows God directly, not from books. And Kashmiris of both faiths also call her Lal Ded, Granny Lalla. There's a story that ties the names together.

teach.h: NUND RISHI ASKS FOR WHAT SHE HAD.
teach.b: Kashmir's Sufi saint Nund Rishi, also called Sheikh Nur-ud-din, founded the order of Rishis, Muslim mystics of the valley. Legend says that as a newborn he wouldn't nurse, until Lalla came and fed him herself.

Grown, he's said to have sung of her: that Lalla of Padmanpur drank her fill of the nectar of God; grant me the same, O God. A Sufi saint, praying to receive what a Shaiva yogini had. Here's the teaching.
In Kashmir, Lalla stands between two traditions, and neither had to give up its own words to honor her. The Shaiva calls her the Lady; the Sufi calls her the one who knows.
The names don't cancel; they each tell you something true about her, and about the people saying them.
So the grandpa's Teddy isn't a mistake to fix. It's his word for love, from before Theo chose his own.

how: Kashmiri Hindus honor her as Lalleshwari and Kashmiri Muslims as Lal Arifa; Nund Rishi, the Sufi saint of the valley, is honored at his shrine at Chrar-e-Sharief, and his verses and hers are recited side by side.

o: a royal title and a name she took as a nun later
a married name and the name she was given at birth
Lalleshwari to Hindus and Lal Arifa to Muslims

games.q: the names and who says them: tap the pairs.
p: Lalla the Lady, a Hindu name
the one who knows God, a Muslim name
Granny Lalla, said in both faiths
Sufi saint who asked for what she had

s: Lal Arifa is a lesser nickname, not a real title of honor
both names are titles of honor, each in its own community's words of honor.
in Sufi language, an arif knows God directly
not from books: one who knows. that's why Muslims call her Lal Arifa.
Nund Rishi was a Shaiva yogi like Lalla
he was a Sufi, founder of Kashmir's Rishi order, and he honored her.

games.q: your friend's grandmother still calls her by a childhood nickname nobody else uses. your friend asks you whether to correct her. what does Lalla's story offer?
o: correct her gently; one true name matters most
drop both names and pick a new neutral one
hear it as the grandmother's word for love
games.why: Lalla's names don't cancel each other: each community honored her in its own words. a name can be someone's way of loving.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose name you've heard said more than one way: a nickname, a family name, a name in another language. Say each version out loud, slowly, the way the people who use it say it.
Then sit, and hear what each one carries.

wordCard.voice: Lalla's two names: Lalleshwari to Hindus, Lal Arifa to Muslims, and Lal Ded, Granny Lalla, to both.

orig.note: Arabic: a woman who knows God directly, from the Sufi word for knowing, ma'rifa. Lal Arifa.

carryVoice: Keep this one: two names, and neither one a mistake. Lalla's days are done; Mira's begin next.

sources.ref: Lalla's names: Lalleshwari, Lal Arifa, Lal Ded (Grierson and Barnett, Lalla-Vakyani, 1920, introduction)
the verse of Nund Rishi (Sheikh Nur-ud-din) on 'that Lalla of Padmanpur' who drank the nectar, and the legend of his nursing (Kashmiri tradition, in Grierson and Barnett's introduction)
